items.scene: A project lead must decide whether to give a confidential client account to an assistant who has been careful and loyal for years but missed one report after a sudden family emergency.
items.question: What is the best judgment of the assistant's reliability right now?
options: Trust the multi-year record and treat the one missed report as an excusable exception.
Treat the assistant as unreliable now because of this one mistake.
Withhold any judgment until the assistant first apologizes for the miss.
Decide solely from the most recent report and ignore the earlier years.
items.why_this_case_matters: Synthetic in-scope item: the call turns on integrating a long track record, where one well-explained lapse should not override years of reliability.

items.scene: A landlord has rented to a tenant for six years with rent paid on time every month. This month the rent arrives one day late because the tenant's bank transfer failed.
items.question: Should the tenant's reliability be downgraded based on this late payment?
options: Yes, one late payment shows the tenant is no longer dependable.
No, the six-year on-time record still supports trusting the tenant.
Yes, but only because a late payment is personally annoying to the landlord.
It cannot be judged at all without a fresh promise from the tenant.
items.why_this_case_matters: Synthetic in-scope item targeting the recency trap: a single isolated, explained deviation should not override a deep, consistent record.

items.scene: Mr. Zhang is a scientist with a high reputation, famous for breakthrough biotechnology research. At a conference someone asks whether he is running a secret project. He replies that he focuses only on publicly published work and does no secret research, stressing that transparency is a core principle of his. In fact he is running a highly confidential government-funded project.
items.question: Why does Mr. Zhang say this?
options: Mr. Zhang says this because he is indeed only conducting publicly published projects and does no secret research.
Mr. Zhang says this because he needs to hide the highly confidential government-funded project he is conducting to protect its safety and confidentiality.
Mr. Zhang recently faces a career crisis and says this to avoid attracting more attention and suspicion.
Mr. Zhang is dissatisfied with his research direction and says this to divert peers' attention and cover up career setbacks.
items.why_this_case_matters: Near miss from ToMBench Strange Story Task (idx 2, gold B): although a reputation is mentioned, the task is to read the motive behind one current statement, not to judge trust from a track record. The reputation is a decoy; this is a single-statement interpretation, so it sits outside track-record judgment.

items.scene: A friend damaged a borrowed bike and offers to replace the parts and apologize. The owner is deciding how to respond so the friendship recovers.
items.question: What is the main issue the owner is dealing with?
options: Whether the friend has built a strong reputation for reliability over time.
How to repair the harm and rebuild trust after the damage already done.
How to split the cost of a shared purchase fairly between them.
Whether this one accident changes the friend's whole identity.
items.why_this_case_matters: Boundary item: harm has already occurred, so the core is apology and repair (option B), not judging trust from a long record (option A) and not a fair-allocation split (option C). It separates this macro from both the repair neighbor and the fairness/reciprocity neighbor.
